title: 9.1–9.3 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 9.1–9.3 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 9.1–9.3.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity that is subject to choice. It does not depend on the other quantity.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad que se elige. No depende de la otra cantidad.
vocabulary.example: The hours of sunlight a tray receives — Akela chooses that.

vocabulary.definition: The quantity that changes in response to the independent variable.
vocabulary.definitionEs: La cantidad que cambia en respuesta a la variable independiente.
vocabulary.example: The height the plants reach — it responds to the sunlight.

vocabulary.definition: One quantity depends on another when changing the first causes the second to change.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cantidad depende de otra cuando cambiar la primera hace cambiar la segunda.

vocabulary.definition: Something that can be counted or measured.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Algo que se puede contar o medir.
vocabulary.example: Hours of sunlight, centimeters of height, minutes of jogging.
More sunlight goes with taller plants.

vocabulary.definition: A picture on a coordinate plane that shows how two quantities are related.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un dibujo en un plano de coordenadas que muestra cómo se relacionan dos cantidades.
vocabulary.example: The football ticket graph shows cost rising as tickets increase.

vocabulary.definition: A list of matched pairs of values that shows a relationship using numbers.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una lista de pares de valores que muestra una relación usando números.
vocabulary.example: The ticket table pairs 3 tickets with $135.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers written as (x, y) that name one point on a graph. The independent variable comes first.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos números escritos como (x, y) que nombran un punto en la gráfica. La variable independiente va primero.

vocabulary.definition: A mathematical sentence with an equals sign that shows two amounts are the same.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una oración matemática con un signo igual que muestra que dos cantidades son iguales.
vocabulary.example: c = 24.95m says the total cost equals $24.95 times the months.
vocabulary.visual: c = 24.95m means the total cost equals $24.95 times the number of months

vocabulary.definition: A letter that represents a quantity that can change, or vary.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una letra que representa una cantidad que puede cambiar o variar.
vocabulary.example: In c = 24.95m, both m (months) and c (cost) are variables.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 9.1–9.3: 9.1 Explore Relationships Between Two Variables, 9.2 Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables, 9.3 Write Equations to Represent Relationships Between Two Variables. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 9.1–9.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 9.1: The independent variable is subject to choice. The dependent variable changes in response to it. • 9.2: Each row of the table becomes one ordered pair — (independent variable, dependent variable) — plotted as one point on the graph. • 9.3: When the total is the rate times the amount, write it as an equation: dependent variable = rate × independent variable.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 9.1 — Explore Relationships Between Two Variables: The independent variable is subject to choice. The dependent variable changes in response to it.
Lesson 9.2 — Analyze Graphs of Relationships Between Two Variables: Each row of the table becomes one ordered pair — (independent variable, dependent variable) — plotted as one point on the graph.
Lesson 9.3 — Write Equations to Represent Relationships Between Two Variables: When the total is the rate times the amount, write it as an equation: dependent variable = rate × independent variable.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 9.1: Claire burned 123 Calories on a 30-minute jog and 246 Calories on a 60-minute jog.
From 9.2: The tram travels 1,200 feet every minute. Which quantity is independent — time or distance?
From 9.3: A canoe rents for $15 per hour. Which quantity is independent — hours or total cost?

youDo.title: Show you're caught up
lines: The practice below mixes problems from Lessons 9.1–9.3. Each problem is tagged with its lesson number.
Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

explore.label: Two equations: c = 24.95m for the Recreation World gym, and c = 15h for the canoe rental. Drag each statement to the equation it matches.
explore.instructions: Sort all eight cards. Check each total by multiplying the rate by the number of months or hours.

connect.scenario: Diamond is considering using an online music service. She can either purchase songs one at a time or pay to stream songs. Each choice has its own relationship between the number of songs and the total cost.
connect.promptQuestion: Would you recommend that Diamond purchase or stream songs from the online music service?
connect.prompt: Diamond should write an ___ for each option so she can ___ the costs. Each equation uses the ___ as the input and gives the ___ as the output.

check.stem: In Diamond's situation, what should be the independent variable in both equations?
choices: the type of service (purchase or stream)
check.explanation: Total cost depends on how many songs Diamond buys or streams, so the number of songs is independent and total cost is dependent. Price per song is a fixed rate (a constant in the equation, not a variable), and the service type determines WHICH equation to use rather than being a variable inside one.

check.stem: Why does Diamond need TWO separate equations instead of one equation for both options?
choices: Purchasing and streaming likely follow different cost rules (such as a per-song price vs. a flat rate), so each relationship between songs and cost is different
The number of songs is different for each option
One equation can only have one variable
Streaming has no relationship between songs and cost
check.explanation: Purchasing and streaming follow different cost rules, so the relationship between number of songs and total cost differs between them, requiring separate equations. The independent variable (number of songs) is the same idea in both equations, equations regularly have two variables, and streaming still relates cost to how much is used.

check.stem: Once Diamond has both equations, how does she use them to decide which option is better?
choices: Substitute the same number of songs into both equations and compare the two total costs
Add the two equations together to find one combined cost
Pick whichever equation has the smaller numbers written in it, without solving anything
Graph only one equation and assume the other follows the same line
check.explanation: Substituting the same number of songs into both equations lets Diamond compare the actual total costs for that amount of listening. Adding the equations doesn't answer a comparison question, comparing raw coefficients ignores how they combine with the number of songs, and assuming one graph represents both ignores that purchasing and streaming are different relationships.

connect.modelAnswer: Diamond should write one equation for purchasing and one for streaming, defining the variables as the number of songs and the total cost. Then she can substitute the number of songs she expects to listen to into both equations and compare the totals. If she listens to only a few songs, one option may cost less; if she listens to many, the other may be the better deal. The equations let her test any number of songs without building a whole table.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 9.2) On the football ticket graph, what does the point (3, 135) represent?
exitTicket.explanation: The independent variable — number of tickets — comes first in the ordered pair, and 3 × $45 = $135, so the point pairs 3 tickets with a total cost of $135.
hints: Which quantity comes first in an ordered pair — the independent or dependent variable?
The number of tickets is the independent variable here.
Check the arithmetic: what is 3 × 45?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Akela chooses how many hours of sunlight each tray gets. Which is the INDEPENDENT variable?
approaching.explanation: Akela chooses the sunlight, so sunlight is subject to choice — that makes it independent.
choiceFeedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
The number of trays is not one of the two quantities being related here.
The number of seeds is not one of the two quantities being related here.
hints: Which quantity did Akela get to decide?
Sunlight was set by where she put the tray.
The one subject to choice is independent.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.1) In Akela's experiment, which is the DEPENDENT variable?
approaching.explanation: Height responds to how much sunlight the tray received, so height is the dependent variable.
choiceFeedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
The kind of seed was the same for all three trays.
The tray size was the same for all three trays.
hints: Which quantity RESPONDED to the other?
Akela did not choose how tall the plants grew.
The responding quantity is dependent.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.2) Football tickets cost $45 each. What is the total cost of 3 tickets?
approaching.explanation: The total cost is 45 times the number of tickets, and 3 × 45 = 135.
choiceFeedback: That adds 45 + 3 instead of multiplying 45 × 3.
$90 is the cost of 2 tickets, not 3.
$45 is the cost of just 1 ticket.
hints: What is the cost of ONE ticket?
Each of the 3 tickets adds another $45.
Multiply the price of one ticket by the number of tickets.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.2) Which ordered pair belongs on the ticket graph for 2 tickets?
approaching.explanation: The number of tickets goes first, and 2 tickets cost 2 × 45 = 90 dollars, so the point is (2, 90).
choiceFeedback: You reversed the coordinates — the independent variable (tickets) goes first.
$45 is the cost of 1 ticket, not 2.
That adds 45 + 2 instead of multiplying 45 × 2.
hints: Which quantity goes first in the ordered pair?
Tickets is the independent variable, so it comes first.
The second number is 2 × 45.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Recreation World charges $24.95 per month. What is the total cost of 2 months of membership?
choiceFeedback: That adds 24.95 + 2 instead of multiplying 24.95 × 2.
$24.95 is the cost of just 1 month.
$74.85 is the cost of 3 months, not 2.
hints: What does ONE month cost?
The second month adds another $24.95.
Multiply 24.95 by 2.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 9.3) In the equation c = 24.95m for the gym membership, what does m represent?
choices: The number of months of membership
approaching.explanation: m stands for the quantity Miguel chooses — the number of months. The letter c stands for the total cost that results.
choiceFeedback: The total cost is represented by c, not m.
$24.95 is the fixed rate written as a number in the equation — it does not need a letter.
Variables stand for quantities that can be counted or measured, not names.
hints: Which letters are variables here — and which quantity does each stand for?
c is the cost. What is left for m?
m counts the months.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.1) A gym charges $24.95 per month. Which pair correctly names the variables?
onLevel.explanation: You choose how many months to stay a member. The total cost responds to that.
choiceFeedback: You have the two variables backward. Ask which one someone gets to CHOOSE — that one is independent.
$24.95 is a fixed rate, not a variable that changes.
$24.95 is a fixed rate, not the responding quantity.
hints: Which number can the member change?
Months is the choice.
Cost responds to months.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Claire jogs 30 minutes and burns 123 Calories. At the same rate, how many Calories would a 90-minute jog burn?
onLevel.explanation: 30 minutes burned 123 Calories, and 90 is 3 times 30, so the Calories are 3 times 123, which is 369.
choiceFeedback: 246 Calories is the 60-minute jog, not the 90-minute jog.
That is not the result of tripling 123.
That is a rounded guess — scale 123 by the same factor as the time.
hints: How many times longer is 90 minutes than 30 minutes?
90 divided by 30 is 3.
Multiply 123 by 3.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.2) The Sandia Peak tram travels 1,200 feet each minute and the ascent takes 15 minutes. How long is the whole ascent in feet?
choiceFeedback: That adds 1,200 + 15 instead of multiplying 1,200 × 15.
12,000 feet is the distance after 10 minutes, not the full 15.
16,800 feet is the distance after 14 minutes — one minute short of the top.
hints: How many minutes does the full ascent take?
Each of those 15 minutes covers 1,200 feet.
Multiply 1,200 by 15.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.2) On the tram graph with minutes on the horizontal axis and feet on the vertical axis, which ordered pair lies on the graph?
onLevel.explanation: After 5 minutes the tram has traveled 5 × 1,200 = 6,000 feet, so the point is (5, 6000).
choiceFeedback: You reversed the coordinates — time (the independent variable) goes first.
1,200 feet is the distance for 1 minute, not 5.
5,000 rounds the rate to 1,000 feet per minute — the tram travels 1,200 feet each minute.
hints: Which axis is time on?
The second coordinate is the distance after 5 minutes.
Multiply 5 by 1,200.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Using c = 24.95m, what is the total cost of 10 months of membership?
choiceFeedback: That adds 24.95 + 10 instead of multiplying 24.95 × 10.
$224.55 is the cost of 9 months — one month short.
That moved the decimal too far: multiplying by 10 shifts the decimal ONE place.
hints: Replace m with 10.
Multiplying by 10 moves the decimal point one place.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Using c = 15h, what is the total cost of a 5-hour canoe rental?
choiceFeedback: That adds 15 + 5 instead of multiplying 15 × 5.
$60 is the cost of 4 hours, not 5.
$80 would need a rate of $16 per hour — the canoe is $15 per hour.
hints: Replace h with 5.
Count by 15s five times.

extending.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Two quantities are related. Which statement is ALWAYS true?
choices: The independent variable is subject to choice
The independent variable is always the larger number
The dependent variable is always measured in dollars
The independent variable is always listed first in a table
extending.explanation: Being subject to choice is the definition. Size, units, and table position are not part of it.
choiceFeedback: A choice can be a small number — 1 hour is independent just as much as 100 hours.
Dependent variables can be centimeters, Calories, miles — anything that responds.
Table layout is a convention, not a definition.
hints: Which option restates the definition?
Definitions do not depend on size or units.
Choice is the deciding test.

extending.stem: (Lesson 9.2) Nakai's savings account has a principal of $750 and earns 3.5% simple interest each year. How much interest does Nakai earn in one year?
extending.explanation: One year of interest is 3.5% of $750: 0.035 × 750 = 26.25.
choiceFeedback: That is 35% of $750 — the decimal point for 3.5% is one place further left.
That treats 3.5% as $3.50 flat instead of taking 3.5% OF the $750 principal.
That is 10% of $750, not 3.5%.
hints: Write 3.5% as a decimal.
Multiply 0.035 by 750.

extending.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Miguel wants the cost of a full year (12 months) at Recreation World. Using c = 24.95m, what is the total?
choiceFeedback: $249.50 is the cost of 10 months, not 12.
That adds 24.95 + 12 instead of multiplying 24.95 × 12.
Close, but that rounds the fee up to $25 — the exact total is 24.95 × 12.
hints: How many months are in a year?
Multiply 24.95 by 12.
Break it up: 24.95 × 10 plus 24.95 × 2.

practice.commonMistake: Writing the equation with addition — c = 24.95 + m — instead of multiplication. The fee is charged EVERY month, so the total is the rate times the number of months; always test the equation against a row of the table.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

parallelPractice.stem: (Lesson 9.1) Complete a new equivalent ratio: 2:3 = ___:___. Use a scale factor of 2.
hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
Start like this: Multiply 2 × 2: 4.
parallelPractice.explanation: Multiply 2 × 2: 4. Multiply 3 × 2: 6. Write the equivalent ratio: 4:6.
parallelPractice.stemEs: Completa una nueva razón equivalente: 2:3 = ___:___. Usa un factor de escala de 2.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta. ¿Qué te pide encontrar exactamente?
Usa el modelo visual y completa un paso a la vez.
Empieza así: Multiplica 2 × 2: 4.
parallelPractice.explanationEs: Multiplica 2 × 2: 4. Multiplica 3 × 2: 6. Escribe la razón equivalente: 4:6.

parallelPractice.stem: (Lesson 9.3) Write an equation: a number x plus 2 equals 4.

steps.promptEs: Usa x para el valor desconocido: ___.

hints: Re-read the question. What exactly is it asking you to find?
Use the visual model, then complete one step at a time.
Start like this: Use x for the unknown: x.
parallelPractice.explanation: Use x for the unknown: x. “plus 2” becomes + 2. Write the equation: x + 2 = 4.
parallelPractice.stemEs: Escribe una ecuación: un número x más 2 es igual a 4.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta. ¿Qué te pide encontrar exactamente?
